title: Bands, in the right order

prereqs.why: The whole problem is an else-if chain, and the order of its tests is the thing that makes it right or wrong.
You need main, std::cin and std::cout, which you already have.

statement:
Read one integer `score` and print the band it falls in:

| Score | Print |
| --- | --- |
| 70 to 100 | `distinction` |
| 60 to 69 | `merit` |
| 40 to 59 | `pass` |
| 0 to 39 | `fail` |
| anything outside 0-100 | `invalid` |

```
input:   73          input:   40          input:   -5
output:  distinction  output:  pass        output:  invalid
```

### The point of the problem

An **else-if chain** tests its conditions in order and stops at the first true
one. That means `score >= 40` is a perfectly good test for "pass" *provided*
the higher bands were already ruled out above it. Get the order wrong and
every score becomes `pass`.

So write it as a chain rather than as four separate `if` statements, and put
the bands in an order where each test only has to exclude what is below it.

### Boundary cases, which are most of the work

`70`, `69`, `60`, `59`, `40`, `39`, `0`, `100`, `101` and `-1` are all
different answers here, and off-by-one at any boundary is the commonest way to
get this wrong. The hidden tests include every one of them. Work out on paper
what each should print before you write the chain.
hints: Rule out the invalid range first, with a single condition using `||`. Then the chain only has to deal with scores you know are between 0 and 100.
Test the bands from the top down: `>= 70`, then `>= 60`, then `>= 40`, then everything left is `fail`. Each test only needs its own lower bound, because the ones above already returned.
Four separate `if` statements would print several lines for one score. The word you need between them is `else`.
